eoce-048.title: The Hawaiian–Emperor bend: the Pacific plate turns
eoce-048.text: A sharp elbow in a line of undersea volcanoes records the moment a whole plate changed direction. The kink in the Hawaiian–Emperor seamount chain marks the Pacific plate's sudden swing from northward to northwestward motion about 47 million years ago. The change followed the onset of subduction along the plate's western edge. A wider reorganization of Pacific plate motions started the Izu-Bonin-Mariana and Tonga-Kermadec subduction zones. Several causes may have combined to make the bend. A northward pull ended around 47 million years ago, and the hotspot itself had drifted south from about 50 million years ago. The new western subduction zones added their own tug.

eoce-046.title: Baltic amber, the great insect vault
eoce-046.text: The biggest single store of fossil insects on Earth is made of tree resin. Baltic amber, the largest amber deposit anywhere, preserves invertebrates, plants and small vertebrates of a subtropical eastern European forest. Its exact age is controversial. Estimates include 47–40 and 43–35 million years ago. Two other major European ambers, from Bitterfeld in Germany and Rovno in Ukraine, date to 38–34 million years ago and share much of its fauna.

eoce-050.title: Kishenehn's blood-filled mosquito
eoce-050.text: A mosquito from Montana died with its last meal still inside it. Oil shale there, about 46.2 million years old, preserves exquisitely detailed insects. Among them is a blood-filled mosquito with traces of hemoglobin, the oxygen-carrying molecule in blood, still detectable after tens of millions of years.

eoce-052.title: Silverpit, a disputed crater under the North Sea
eoce-052.text: Under the North Sea, about 130 km off the Humber estuary, lies a buried structure that looks like a crater. Whether it is one is still argued. A 2025 study says yes: an impact crater about 3.2 km wide, ringed by an 18 km disturbed zone, formed 46–43 million years ago. Others attribute it to moving underground salt, an explanation favored in a 2009 debate. Its impact origin remains disputed.

eoce-054.title: The Andes rise and the Altiplano forms
eoce-054.text: One of the highest plateaus on Earth began forming in the Eocene. Subduction beneath South America compressed the plate's edge, and the Altiplano started to rise. The high Central Andes and the Bolivian orocline, the great bend in the mountain chain, formed from about 45 million years ago. Major uplift in southern Peru began then too. In northern Peru, the Incaic phase of mountain building struck in the middle and late Eocene. Peru's Western Cordillera had begun rising about 50 million years ago, then paused until the Oligocene. Ever since, the region around the Altiplano and Puna plateaus has been shortened horizontally.

eoce-057.title: The Tasmanian Passage opens
eoce-057.text: When Australia pulled away from Antarctica, the southern oceans changed course. In one account, the two split around 45 million years ago. Warm equatorial currents were diverted, and a cold-water channel opened between them. The South Tasman Rise had already sunk beneath the sea, forming the Tasmanian Passage. As oceanic crust began separating the continents about 35.5 million years ago, global ocean temperatures dropped significantly. The dates are contested. The general consensus is that the continents had fully separated by 60 million years ago, and 45 million is a minority estimate. A 2013 paper dates the first flow through the gateway, and the cooling, to about 49–50 million years ago.

eoce-056.title: The Quercy 'natural mummies'
eoce-056.text: In southern France, cracks in limestone became time capsules. Karst fissures, cavities dissolved in the rock, filled with sediment holding mammals, birds, turtles, crocodiles, plants and insects from about 45–25 million years ago. Some amphibians and lizards survive as articulated 'natural mummies', with their soft tissue preserved.

eoce-058.title: India and Australia fuse into one plate
eoce-058.text: Two of the plates that had drifted apart from Gondwana ended up joined again. The Indo-Australian plate formed when the Indian and Australian plates fused, approximately 43 million years ago. From then on they moved as a single slab of crust.

eoce-059.title: The Logoisk crater in Belarus
eoce-059.text: Belarus hides a buried crater 15 km wide. A meteorite struck near the town of Lahoysk about 42.3 million years ago and left it. Today it lies beneath younger sediment, invisible at the surface.

eoce-060.title: A burst of magnetic reversals
eoce-060.text: Around 42 million years ago, Earth's magnetic field could not settle down. It flipped 17 times in 3 million years, swapping north and south again and again. That was a fast pace. Earlier, in a 4-million-year window centered on 54 million years ago, there were 10 reversals, a contrast with the long calm of {{ref:cret-115}}.

eoce-061.title: Basilosaurus, the giant fully marine whale
eoce-061.text: Basilosaurus was a whale, and a huge one. This large predatory archaeocete, an early whale, lived from about 41.3 to 33.9 million years ago. At 17–20 m and up to 15 tonnes, it was one of the largest animals of the Paleogene. It was a top predator of shallow seas, eating sharks, large fish and other marine mammals, especially the smaller whale Dorudon. By the end of the Eocene, whales such as Basilosaurus had become fully aquatic. Its extinction coincides with {{ref:eoce-095}}, which ended almost all other archaeocetes.

eoce-062.title: The Drake Passage begins to open
eoce-062.text: South America and Antarctica were once joined by land. In the early Eocene the Drake Passage, the gap between them, was only a small opening with limited circulation. When it widened is uncertain, with estimates running from 49 to 17 million years ago. Sediments suggest it began opening about 41 million years ago, while tectonic evidence points to about 32 million. The Scotia plate began forming about 40 million years ago, breaking the continuous land from Patagonia to the Antarctic Peninsula. Cooling during the first opening, about 38.5 million years ago, was not global, since the North Atlantic did not cool. Together the Drake and Tasmanian passages ended the Antarctic land bridge in the late Eocene or early Oligocene.

eoce-063.title: The Middle Eocene Climatic Optimum
eoce-063.text: For half a million years, the long Eocene cooling went into reverse. From about 40.5 to 40.0 million years ago, a spell of very warm climate interrupted the slide. The warming happened everywhere at once. Mean surface temperature reached about 23 °C, and the Tethys Sea's surface reached 32–36 °C. Carbon dioxide drove it, not methane. One estimate puts CO2 at 4,000 ppm, though other studies find a smaller rise. A minimum in two orbital eccentricity cycles, around 40.2 million years ago, likely helped sustain the warmth. Planktonic foraminifera turned over: acarinids dwindled and morozovellids went extinct.

eoce-064.title: Balkanatolia, a lost continent, joins Asia
eoce-064.text: About 50 million years ago, Eurasia was not one landmass but three: Western Europe, Balkanatolia and Asia. Balkanatolia, the land that became the Balkans and Anatolia, joined Asia about 40 million years ago. Europe connected only about 34 million years ago. Asian mammals poured in, and they may have driven Balkanatolia's island-like native fauna extinct.

eoce-065.title: The Eridanos, a lost Baltic river
eoce-065.text: Where the Baltic Sea now lies, a great river once flowed. The Eridanos, an ancient river through what is now the Baltic region, began to form about 40 million years ago. Today the Baltic Sea covers the land it once drained.

eoce-067.title: Mesohippus, a horse for open country
eoce-067.text: As forests thinned, horses had to run. About 40 million years ago Mesohippus appeared suddenly, under strong new selective pressures. Late Eocene horses grew tougher teeth and became larger and leggier, able to outrun predators in open country. Miohippus followed around 36 million years ago, continuing the line from {{ref:eoce-027}}.

eoce-071.title: Rodents and monkeys raft across the Atlantic
eoce-071.text: Some of South America's most famous animals arrived as castaways. About 40 million years ago, caviomorph rodents reached South America, most likely from Africa. Primates followed by 36 million years ago, crossing the same way. The ocean gap was narrower then. Animals floated over on rafts of driftwood or mangrove, perhaps hopping between islands. The rodents gave rise to capybaras, chinchillas and New World porcupines, displacing some small marsupials. Today the descendants of these rafters make up more than twice as many South American species as those of older native mammals.

eoce-070.title: Rifting begins in northern Kenya
eoce-070.text: East Africa began to crack open in the Eocene. Volcanism and rifting began around Turkana, in northern Kenya, 40–35 million years ago. The rifting then spread north and south along the Gregory Rift.

eoce-068.title: The mid-Tertiary ignimbrite flare-up
eoce-068.text: From about 40 to 25 million years ago, the western United States went through one of Earth's great volcanic outbursts. The eruptions, of andesite to rhyolite lava, produced about 500,000 km³ of explosive and 5 million km³ of effusive rock. Explosive eruptions blast out ash; effusive ones pour out lava. The flare-up followed the end of Laramide compression, as the Farallon slab steepened and plate motion changed. Colorado's San Juan volcanoes became active 40–35 million years ago. New Mexico's Mogollon-Datil field began erupting about 36.2 million years ago. In Mexico's Sierra Madre Occidental, Oligocene ash flows stacked ignimbrite sheets, layers of welded volcanic ash, over the largest area of any known series, with ten calderas.

eoce-076.title: The last multituberculates
eoce-076.text: The longest-reigning mammals of all finally bowed out in the late Eocene. Multituberculates had dominated most mammal assemblages for at least 88 million years, in a lineage that went back to the Jurassic. They had declined since the mid-Paleocene, as {{ref:pale-011}} describes. The last species, Ectypodus childei, died out in North America near the end of the Eocene, possibly outcompeted by rodents. Only the gondwanatheres outlived them. One account has them lasting into the early Oligocene. Around 35 million years ago, extinctions also struck gastropods, reptiles and amphibians.

eoce-078.title: Lake Wanapitei impact
eoce-078.text: A round lake in Canada fills the scar of an impact. About 37.2 million years ago, a body from space struck and made a crater 8.4 km across. Today that crater holds Lake Wanapitei.

eoce-079.title: The Cascade volcanoes awaken
eoce-079.text: The volcanic arc that includes today's Cascade peaks began to burn about 37 million years ago. Volcanism in the Cascade arc of the Pacific Northwest began then. The West Cascades period that followed, from 37 to 17 million years ago, was a time of exceptionally active volcanoes.

eoce-080.title: Ice sheets begin to grow on Antarctica
eoce-080.text: By the late Eocene, about 37 million years ago, Antarctica had grown cold enough to hold ice sheets. Oxygen isotopes show ice building up from about 36 million years ago, and permanent ice from about 35 million years ago. Around 35 million years ago, glaciers merged into the East Antarctic Ice Sheet. It buried the Gamburtsev Mountains, which remain hidden under the ice. A brief glaciation, the Late Eocene Event, followed about 34.4 million years ago.

eoce-082.title: The White River fauna
eoce-082.text: Beavers, squirrels and gophers took over North America as the tropics retreated. In North America's Chadronian age, from 37 million years ago, the White River fauna was in full swing. Modern rodent families replaced older tropical ones, alongside early relatives of bears, peccaries and rabbits. The rabbit relatives had come from East Asia, reaching North America in the late Eocene.

eoce-083.title: The Mistastin impact in Labrador
eoce-083.text: In the wilds of Labrador, Canada, lies a crater that was once about 28 km across. An impact made it about 36.6 million years ago, one of several large strikes of the late Eocene.

eoce-084.title: Popigai, a giant crater in Siberia
eoce-084.text: In northern Siberia lies one of the largest scars ever left by a rock from space. In the late Eocene, a large bolide, an exploding meteor, blasted a 100 km crater there. It is tied as the fourth-largest verified impact structure on Earth. It may be linked to {{ref:eoce-095}}. It may also have struck at the same time as the Chesapeake Bay and Toms Canyon impacts.

eoce-085.title: The Chesapeake Bay impact
eoce-085.text: The shape of Chesapeake Bay owes something to a rock from space. A bolide about 3 km wide struck the eastern shore of North America, then lined with rainforest and shallow limy seas. It left a crater about 85 km wide, now buried beneath the mouth of Chesapeake Bay. It is one of the best-preserved craters made in the sea. Sediment slumping over its rubble helped shape the bay. The nearby Toms Canyon crater, and possibly Siberia's {{ref:eoce-084}}, may have formed in the same event.

eoce-087.title: The Laramide orogeny ends
eoce-087.text: The mountain building that raised the Rockies finally wound down, though no one agrees exactly when. The Laramide orogeny, active since the Late Cretaceous, ended sometime between 55 and 35 million years ago. In New Mexico, deformation lasted until about 40 million years ago. As convergence slowed, the Farallon slab steepened and plate motion turned oblique. Volcanism flared across the Basin and Range. Compression gave way to crustal stretching, which in time formed the Basin and Range Province. The orogeny's exact start and end dates remain in dispute.

eoce-088.title: Mountain belts rise around the Mediterranean
eoce-088.text: Many of the Mediterranean's mountain ranges were born in a single burst of collisions. About 35 million years ago, Adria's Anatolide–Tauride platform entered the subduction trench, beginning the Dinarides, Hellenides and Taurides. Between about 40 and 30 million years ago, subduction began along the western Mediterranean arc of the Tell, Rif, Betic and Apennine chains. The Central and Western Alps formed in a second phase of mountain building, starting at the end of the Eocene, 35 million years ago.

eoce-089.title: The Ring of Fire takes its modern shape
eoce-089.text: The Pacific's ring of volcanoes is surprisingly young in its present form. By about 35 million years ago, the Kula and Farallon plates had been subducted. The Pacific plate was then ringed by subduction much like today's Ring of Fire. The New Zealand subduction zone, the last of its present segments, formed about 35 million years ago.

eoce-086.title: Arabia collides with Eurasia and the Zagros rise
eoce-086.text: The mountains of Iran mark where Arabia rammed into Asia. Continental collision between Arabia and Eurasia began about 35 million years ago and continued into the Oligocene, to about 26 million years ago. It closed the Tethys Ocean there and created the Zagros Mountains. Earlier, during the Eocene, a sinking slab of Neotethys ocean floor had broken off near the Arabian margin.

eoce-090.title: EOT-1: the first step into the ice age
eoce-090.text: Around 34 million years ago, the long cooling crossed a threshold. As carbon dioxide fell, a large ice sheet formed in East Antarctica. Antarctica glaciated in two steps. The first and smaller, EOT-1, came about 34.1–33.9 million years ago, at the Eocene–Oligocene boundary itself. Glaciers sliding off the Gamburtsev Mountains are thought to have seeded the East Antarctic Ice Sheet. By the boundary, an ice sheet in western Antarctica reached the ocean, and glaciers had appeared in Greenland. The oceans changed too. As the Arctic–Atlantic gateway closed, deep overturning circulation shifted from the Pacific to the Atlantic.

eoce-092.title: Florissant, a lake of fossils
eoce-092.text: In Colorado, a lake dammed by volcanic mudflows became a perfect fossil trap. Diatom blooms in its water finely preserved late Eocene plants and insects, about 34 million years ago. The site is also famous for petrified stumps of giant sequoia relatives.

eoce-094.title: Toothed and baleen whales go separate ways
eoce-094.text: The great filter-feeding whales began as hunters with teeth. The ancestors of toothed and baleen whales split around 34 million years ago, as the southern oceans' climate changed with the opening of the Drake Passage. The earliest known baleen whale, Mystacodon, 37 to 33 million years old, still had teeth and fed by suction. Later forms carried both baleen and teeth. Then they lost their teeth and became full filter feeders, as all living baleen whales are. Toothed whales are defined by features for echolocation, the use of echoes to sense surroundings, such as a fatty forehead organ called the melon. Oligocene Squalodon skulls give the first hypothesized evidence of it.

eoce-095.title: The Eocene–Oligocene extinction
eoce-095.text: The Eocene closed with the planet flipping from greenhouse to icehouse, and life paid the price. A major extinction and faunal turnover, called the Grande Coupure, or 'great break', in Europe, spanned about 33.9 to 33.4 million years ago. It came with sharp cooling, a big drop in sea level and rapid growth of the Antarctic ice sheet. Carbon dioxide fell to about 750–800 ppm. In the sea, hantkeninid planktonic foraminifera went extinct, and their disappearance marks the boundary. {{ref:eoce-061}} and nearly all other archaic whales died out. In central North America, the cooling turned over snails, amphibians and reptiles. Some sites show extinctions drawn out over millions of years, beginning in the early Priabonian. The causes are debated and not fully understood. The large Popigai and Chesapeake Bay impacts may also have played a part.

openers.eocene-epoch: The Eocene opened in heat. Around its start, oxygen in the atmosphere more or less doubled, and the warmth of the PETM brought modern mammal groups into North America. Primates, songbirds, parrots and loons all appear early in the epoch. India crashed into Eurasia, and Greenland split from Europe. Soon came the EECO, the warmest sustained interval of the whole Cenozoic.

reviews.eocene-epoch: The Eocene ran from the warmest stretch of the Cenozoic to the first great ice sheets on Antarctica. In its hothouse, palms grew in Alaska, and modern mammals, horses, bats and the first whales spread across the world. Then the climate turned around 49 million years ago, helped by the Azolla fern and by new ocean gateways around Antarctica. As carbon dioxide fell and ice grew, the epoch ended in the Eocene–Oligocene extinction, which took Basilosaurus and nearly all archaic whales. The icehouse world that followed is the one that leads to the ice ages.

eoce-056.text: Limestone landscape riddled with cavities and fissures dissolved by water.

eoce-068.text: A layer of volcanic ash welded together by its own heat.

eoce-094.text: Sensing the surroundings by sending out sounds and listening for their echoes.

eoce-084.text: A large meteor that explodes or strikes the ground.
